name: Salesloft
tagline: Sales engagement platform for enterprise revenue teams.
description: Salesloft is a sales engagement platform organized around cadences, conversation review, coaching, and forecasting for revenue teams.
pros: Cadences turn outreach into a repeatable queue, so a rep's day starts with what is due rather than with a plan to construct
Conversation review hands managers evidence for coaching instead of asking them to rely on a rep's recollection of a call
Forecast roll-ups read the same activity record the cadences produce, tying the quarter's number to observable work
The entry band this repository records, $75-200/mo, sits below the band it holds for Outreach
Engagement work stays separate from the CRM, which suits organizations that already have a system of record they trust
cons: Cadence quality depends on an internal owner; without one the queues decay into steps nobody on the team trusts
The category notes in this repository record major CRMs adding native engagement features, so some buyers pay for capability they already hold
No entry for certification, retention terms, or residency options exists in this repository's record for Salesloft

content.title: Salesloft's cadence operating model
content.body: Salesloft is a sales engagement platform built around the cadence: a repeating rhythm of emails, calls, and tasks that keeps a rep's book of business moving on a schedule. What distinguishes it inside this category is where the emphasis falls — not only on executing touches, but on what managers do with the record of them. This repository files Salesloft under CRM & Sales, describes it as a sales engagement platform for enterprise revenue teams, and records a paid band of $75-200/mo. Its own guidance on the category groups Salesloft with platforms that automate outbound sequences, track opens and clicks, and manage sales call activity.

content.title: Cadences and the rep's working day
content.body: A cadence assigns a prospect a sequence of scheduled actions: an email on day one, a call on day two, a break, another attempt later. The rep works from a queue of what is due rather than from a plan they maintain themselves, and completing a step either advances the prospect or drops them out of the rhythm. That queue is the daily surface of the product, and its quality depends entirely on how the cadences were designed. Someone owns the templates, the timing, and the retirement of steps that stop earning replies — which is a management job, not a setup task.
items: An email step that sends or drafts on a scheduled day
A call step that drops a number into the rep's queue
A task step for research, follow-up, or a hand-written note
Breaks between attempts so a prospect is not contacted continuously
Exit rules that pull a prospect out once a reply arrives

content.title: Conversation intelligence and manager coaching
content.body: Recorded conversations and written communication become material for review: calls captured, transcribed, and scored against what good looks like in that organization, so a coaching conversation starts from evidence rather than recollection. Salesloft's position in this repository's field is consistent with that emphasis, since the platform is filed as a revenue-team product where conversation review and manager workflow matter as much as send volume. The picture drawn here is assembled from Salesloft's published documentation and this repository's stored records about the product. Which scoring criteria ship by default, and how much configuration they require, is not captured in these fields.

content.title: Forecasting from the activity record
content.body: The forecasting view reads the same activity and pipeline data toward a different question: what is this quarter going to land at. Deals carry expectations and next steps, roll-ups aggregate what reps report, and the activity record underneath gives a manager a basis for adjusting a number rather than defending one. This repository's category notes describe revenue intelligence as capturing activity automatically and identifying at-risk deals, which is the frame Salesloft's forecasting sits in. The dataset does not record how the forecasting output is derived, how a rep's number and a manager's number reconcile, or which plan carries it.

content.title: Where a cadence platform stops paying off
content.body: Cadence platforms lose their edge in three situations. A small team with a handful of prospects does not need a queue engine — a shared task list does the job with less administration. An organization whose CRM already includes native engagement features is buying overlapping capability, and this repository's own guide observes that modern CRMs are adding exactly those features. And a team unwilling to assign an owner for cadence design will watch the product decay into ignored steps, because the value sits in the upkeep rather than in the installation.

content.title: What the $75-200/mo record leaves out
content.body: Recorded under a paid model, Salesloft carries a band of $75-200/mo in this repository — lower at the entry point than the band held for Outreach, and well above the pipeline CRMs the same comparison files cover. Missing from the field: whether the figure is per user, what conversation review costs, and which capabilities require a higher tier. The repository's alternatives file scores Salesloft at 4.3/5, which agrees with this review's own rating field — one of the cleaner alignments in the dataset. Check the vendor’s current published price list before budgeting.

content.title: Sitting beside the CRM rather than replacing it
content.body: Salesloft executes against a record it does not own. Contacts and opportunities come from the CRM, cadence activity returns to it, and the connection between the two is where data quality is won or lost. The guide stored in this repository puts the boundary in plain terms: many CRMs include basic engagement features, but dedicated platforms offer deeper automation for high-volume outbound teams. That is the honest sales pitch — depth in exchange for another integration to maintain. Named connectors are not itemized here, though the comparison files show Salesloft measured against Close CRM, Copper CRM, Pipedrive, Zoho CRM, HubSpot, Salesforce, Freshsales, Zendesk, and Outreach.

content.title: Hosting and the certification gap
content.body: The product is delivered from the vendor's cloud, which is what allows cadence data, recordings, and coaching material to follow reps across devices. What this repository does not hold for Salesloft is a certification, a retention schedule, a residency term, or an identity detail — and coaching material, meaning recordings and transcripts of customer conversations, is precisely the category of data that draws the most scrutiny in a security review. Treat that question as open, answer it from the vendor’s current documentation set set, and do not let the cloud delivery model stand in for it.

content.title: Salesloft beside Outreach, Close, and Pipedrive
content.body: Salesloft's nearest neighbour in this dataset is Outreach: the same category, 4.3/5 against 4.2/5, and $75-200/mo against a higher band held for Outreach. The recorded emphasis differs on each side — Salesloft as a platform for enterprise revenue teams with coaching and forecasting at the center, Outreach as sequence automation and analytics — which reads as a manager-facing product against an execution-facing one. Underneath that pair sit Pipedrive and Close CRM, pipeline tools that do not attempt cadence orchestration, and Zoho CRM, a suite carried at its own recorded band. The Salesloft alternatives file names Pipedrive, Zoho CRM, Close CRM, Outreach, and Copper CRM.

content.title: Who should shortlist Salesloft
content.body: Shortlist Salesloft when the constraint is managerial visibility into a team that already has volume: a manager who wants evidence for coaching, a forecast that rests on recorded activity rather than on opinion, and a cadence structure that keeps reps from improvising their own outreach. It is the wrong purchase for a team of three, for an organization whose CRM already ships engagement features it will actually use, and for buyers who need certification evidence before signature, which these records do not carry. The dataset holds 4.3/5 for Salesloft across 560 recorded reviews.

faqs.question: Is Salesloft a CRM or an engagement platform?
faqs.answer: An engagement platform. It runs cadences, calls, and coaching against contacts and deals that live in a CRM; this repository's category notes describe the pair as system of record and system of action.

faqs.question: How does Salesloft differ from Outreach?
faqs.answer: Both are engagement platforms here. Salesloft is filed as a platform for enterprise revenue teams at $75-200/mo and 4.3/5, with coaching and forecasting emphasized; Outreach as sequence automation and analytics, carried at a higher band, with 4.2/5.

faqs.question: Does Salesloft replace the CRM?
faqs.answer: No. Activity executes in Salesloft and returns to the CRM, so an organization without a record system needs one alongside it. Named connectors are not itemized in this repository.

faqs.question: What is recorded for Salesloft's price?
faqs.answer: A paid model with a band of $75-200/mo, with no indication of per-user structure or of which features require higher tiers. Confirm current list pricing and packaging with the vendor.

faqs.question: What does this repository record about Salesloft security?
faqs.answer: Certifications, retention schedules, and residency terms are missing from the fields held for Salesloft. Coaching recordings make that a question to answer early with the vendor.

author: Sarah Chen
learningCurve: Reps pick up the daily queue quickly; cadence design, conversation scoring criteria, and forecast configuration are where the time goes.
whoShouldUse: Revenue teams with real outbound volume and a manager whose job includes coaching, organizations that want a forecast grounded in recorded activity, and enterprises that prefer engagement tooling kept separate from their CRM.
whoShouldNotUse: Small teams that need little more than a shared task list, buyers whose CRM already ships engagement features they will use, and organizations that require certification evidence before purchase, which this dataset does not carry.
